R060-01.notes: Passage A reports traffic drops in London and Stockholm and closes with the lesson that drivers respond to prices and that 'the benefits of a charge are easier to see once people have lived with it,' which matches A. B: the passage never ranks London against Stockholm; it calls Stockholm 'especially telling' but makes no success comparison. C: directly contradicted by 'The lesson is not that a price solves every transportation problem.' D: the opposition before the vote is one detail, not the main purpose.

R060-02.notes: The vote came 'after seven months of shorter commutes,' following earlier opposition, so it supports the claim that benefits become easier to see with experience. A: contradicted by 'Before the trial, most residents opposed the charge.' B: the passage makes no claim about the best way to decide policy. D: the immediate traffic drop came before the vote, and the vote does not explain it; this reverses cause and effect.

R060-03.notes: Nearly verbatim: trips were 'shifted to other hours, combined, or made by bus.' A: rerouting is the gridlock prediction that did not happen. B: nothing about drivers being unable to afford the charge. C: trips moved onto buses; walking and crowding are never mentioned. This is a straightforward detail item.

R060-04.notes: The example illustrates the sentence before it: 'a fee that is the same for everyone is not the same burden for everyone.' A: the passage gives no driving frequencies. C: B never proposes exemptions. D: B says 'No one seriously disputes that a congestion charge can cut traffic.'

R060-05.notes: B says 'their fairness depends on what a city does with the money and on what alternatives it offers.' A: contradicted by 'This does not mean that charges are a mistake' and by the bus-revenue example of a fairer design. B: this is the supporters' view, which the author rejects. C: B warns that referendum support is not proof of fairness and never makes a referendum a requirement.

R060-06.notes: The context glosses the word: 'neutral: everyone pays the same fee, and everyone benefits.' B, C and D are other dictionary senses of 'neutral' (electrical, political or military, and color) that do not fit the context. The item is easy but works.

R060-07.notes: B's last paragraph: early public support is not 'proof that a charge treats everyone well,' and voters 'are not always the ones who bear the heaviest costs.' A: the opposite of B's view. C: overstates B, which questions what the vote shows, not whether it was valid, and never mentions non-drivers. D: B concedes that charges cut traffic.

R060-08.notes: A shows trips shifted in time, combined, or moved to buses. B says no one disputes that charges cut traffic, and cutting traffic requires that people travel differently, so both authors would accept C. A: B rejects it and A never claims it. B: A never discusses revenue, and B does not rank revenue above the traffic effect. D: B rejects it and A does not say it.

R060-09.notes: B contrasts a charge whose revenue improves bus service with one whose revenue 'disappears into a general budget.' A: the passage gives no traffic difference. C: 'identical at the toll gantry' implies the same fee, so C contradicts the passage. D: referendums are not part of this comparison.

R060-10.notes: B is about how the burden is distributed: the lawyer versus the aide, and voters who are not the ones bearing the costs. B: B treats the traffic reduction as undisputed; A focuses on it more. C: the history of London and Stockholm is A's focus. D: the economic theory of pricing road space is in A's opening paragraph.
